content: FOREST, an acronym for Freedom Organisation for the Right to Enjoy Smoking Tobacco, is a political pressure group based in the United Kingdom. Its primary mission is to advocate for the rights of individuals to smoke tobacco, oppose efforts to ban or reduce tobacco consumption, and challenge medical claims regarding the health risks associated with smoking. The group describes itself as the voice and friend of the smoker and is predominantly funded by the tobacco industry. FOREST was officially established in 1979 by Sir Christopher Foxley-Norris, a former Air Chief Marshal. In 1987, Lord Harris of High Cross, who served as the general director of the Institute of Economic Affairs from 1957 to 1989, was appointed as chairman. He held this position until his death in October 2006 at the age of 81. Lord Harris, a long-time pipe smoker and vocal critic of public smoking bans, authored numerous articles and essays on the topic of passive smoking, also referred to as second-hand smoke, sidestream smoke, or environmental tobacco smoke. One of his notable works, Smoking Out The Truth: a challenge to the Chief Medical Officer (2005), questioned prevailing medical narratives about the dangers of passive smoking. FOREST representatives frequently appear on television and radio in the UK and are often quoted in British newspapers. The organization’s website acknowledges that it is funded mainly by the tobacco industry. Critics have alleged that FOREST is an astroturf group created by the tobacco industry, with its establishment reportedly planned by the Tobacco Advisory Committee, the trade association for the British tobacco industry. Meeting minutes from the Public Relations Sub-Committee of the Tobacco Advisory Committee in August 1979 suggest that the creation of FOREST was discussed prior to its official founding. In recent years, FOREST has garnered support from several prominent smokers, including artist David Hockney, inventor Trevor Baylis, musician Joe Jackson, restaurateur and TV chef Antony Worrall Thompson, and Claire Fox, director of the Institute of Ideas. In September 2005, Hockney, Jackson, and Fox spoke at a fringe meeting organized by FOREST during the Labour Party conference in Brighton. In February 2006, FOREST lost its campaign against a comprehensive ban on smoking in enclosed public spaces in England, which came into effect in the summer of 2007. This ban extended to all pubs, bars, cafés, restaurants, workplaces, and private members' clubs. Similar bans were implemented in Northern Ireland (spring 2007) and Wales (April 2007), while Scotland introduced its own public smoking ban in March 2006. Despite these setbacks, FOREST has pledged to continue advocating for what it terms freedom of choice. The group’s current slogans include Smokers are voters, too, Enough is enough, and Nanny state? No thanks.
